question_text: A company wants to systematically compare three candidate FMs on their specific task (customer email response quality) using automated metrics across a test dataset. Which AWS feature enables this?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Autopilot
Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluations
Amazon Comprehend classification jobs
AWS Glue DataBrew profiling jobs

explanation: Skill 5.1.2 cites Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluations for systematic model evaluation. Bedrock Model Evaluations supports human (crowd-sourced or internal) and automated evaluations across multiple metrics (relevance, coherence, fluency, accuracy), enabling objective multi-model comparison on custom datasets. SageMaker Autopilot is for traditional ML AutoML. Comprehend classification is for supervised NLP tasks. Glue DataBrew is for structured data profiling.
source_topic: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluations

question_text: A team needs to evaluate whether FM-generated customer support responses are helpful, accurate, and professional at scale — without human labellers for every response. Which evaluation approach scales this?

options.text: Sample 10 responses randomly per week and grade them manually
Use an LLM-as-a-Judge approach — configure a judge FM that evaluates each response against helpfulness, accuracy, and professionalism rubrics
Use BLEU or ROUGE scores against a reference answer corpus
Measure response length — longer responses indicate higher quality

explanation: Skill 5.1.5 describes automated quality assessment with LLM-as-a-Judge techniques. A capable judge FM (e.g., Claude) evaluates each response against a structured rubric — scalable, consistent, and available in Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluations as an automated evaluator. Weekly random sampling has high variance and misses systematic failures. BLEU/ROUGE score lexical overlap — poor proxies for conversational quality. Response length has no correlation with quality.
source_topic: LLM-as-a-Judge, automated evaluation, Bedrock

question_text: A team is evaluating their RAG system. They need to measure both retrieval quality and generation quality. Which metrics cover both components? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Context Recall — the proportion of relevant information from the knowledge base that was successfully retrieved
Answer Faithfulness — whether the generated answer is grounded in the retrieved context (not hallucinated)
FM parameter count — larger models produce higher RAG scores
Token latency — faster retrieval indicates better RAG quality
Embedding model release date — newer embeddings always retrieve better

explanation: Skill 5.1.5 and 5.1.6 describe RAG evaluation covering retrieval quality and context matching. Context Recall measures retrieval completeness (did we retrieve all relevant chunks?). Answer Faithfulness measures generation quality (does the answer stay grounded in retrieved context?). RAGAS and similar frameworks operationalise both. Parameter count doesn't predict RAG-specific quality. Token latency measures speed — not retrieval/generation quality. Embedding recency is irrelevant — quality depends on domain fit, not release date.
source_topic: RAG evaluation, context recall, answer faithfulness, RAGAS

question_text: A team wants to deploy an updated FM version but is concerned about quality regression. They want to test it on a small fraction of real production traffic before full rollout. Which deployment pattern supports this?

options.text: Deploy the new model to all users simultaneously and roll back if issues arise
Use canary testing — route 5% of production traffic to the new model, monitor quality metrics, and gradually increase the percentage if metrics stay within thresholds
Deploy to production on a Friday afternoon to minimise business impact if something goes wrong
Use Amazon SageMaker Autopilot to automatically select the best model version

explanation: Skill 5.1.2 cites canary testing of FMs. Canary deployments route a small traffic percentage to the new model, monitor quality and error metrics, and progressively increase the canary weight — limiting blast radius if the new model underperforms. Full simultaneous rollout exposes all users to regression risk. Weekend deployments mask monitoring data. SageMaker Autopilot is for traditional ML model selection, not FM deployment strategy.
source_topic: Canary testing, FM deployment, quality gates

question_text: A team built a multi-step AI agent for customer order management. How should they evaluate whether the agent completes tasks correctly and uses tools efficiently?

options.text: Evaluate only the final output — task completion rate is sufficient
Use Amazon Bedrock Agent Evaluations to assess task completion rate, tool usage effectiveness, and reasoning quality across multi-step scenarios
Measure response latency — faster agents are better agents
Count the number of tool calls — fewer calls always means better performance

explanation: Skill 5.1.7 cites Amazon Bedrock Agent Evaluations for task completion rate measurements, tool usage effectiveness evaluations, and reasoning quality assessment in multi-step workflows. Evaluating only final output misses intermediate reasoning errors and inefficient tool use. Latency measures speed — not correctness. Fewer tool calls is sometimes more efficient, but an agent that skips necessary tool calls produces incorrect results — completeness matters more than count.
source_topic: Amazon Bedrock Agent Evaluations, agent evaluation

question_text: Before promoting a new FM version to production, a team wants automated checks that validate response consistency and detect semantic drift versus the previous version. Which approach implements this as a quality gate in CI/CD?

options.text: Review responses manually in a staging environment
Run synthetic user workflow tests against the new FM version; compute semantic similarity of responses versus golden references; fail the gate if similarity drops below threshold
Check that the new FM version has more parameters than the old one
Verify that the new model's API endpoint is reachable

explanation: Skill 5.1.9 describes deployment validation systems using synthetic user workflows and AI-specific output validation for hallucination rates and semantic drift. Automated semantic similarity tests against golden responses provide an objective, repeatable quality gate in CI/CD — far more reliable than manual review. Parameter count doesn't predict output quality. API reachability is a health check — not a quality gate.
source_topic: Deployment validation, semantic drift, quality gates, CI/CD

question_text: A company wants to collect structured user feedback on FM response quality (thumbs up/down + optional comment) to build a dataset for continuous model improvement. Which approach implements this?

options.text: Monitor CloudWatch error rates as a proxy for user satisfaction
Add a feedback UI (thumbs up/down, optional text) to the application; store feedback records with the original prompt and response in DynamoDB for analysis
Use Amazon Rekognition sentiment analysis on user facial expressions during chat sessions
Automatically infer satisfaction from FM response token count

explanation: Skill 5.1.3 describes feedback interfaces and rating systems for model outputs. A structured feedback UI captures direct user signals; storing them linked to the original prompt/response in DynamoDB creates a labelled dataset for RLHF, prompt tuning, or evaluation. Error rates don't measure perceived quality. Facial recognition during chat is invasive, unreliable, and out of scope. Token count has no relationship to user satisfaction.
source_topic: User feedback, RLHF, annotation workflow

question_text: A company is replacing its production translation FM with a new candidate model. The process must be sequential and each step reviewed before the next. Place the following steps in the correct order: (A) Conduct A/B testing; (B) Create test dataset; (C) Define evaluation metrics; (D) Implement automated quality gates via Step Functions; (E) Analyse results and generate report.

options.text: C → B → A → D → E
B → C → A → E → D
A → B → C → D → E
C → A → B → D → E

explanation: Skill 5.1.2 describes systematic model evaluation systems. The correct sequence is: (C) Define metrics first — establish what 'good' looks like (the yardstick); (B) Create test dataset — build the 'test paper' with diverse cases, shared to both models; (A) Conduct A/B testing — put both models through the test; (D) Implement automated quality gates via Step Functions — 'machine judge' enforces thresholds and requires human approval before promoting; (E) Analyse and generate report — compile evidence for decision-making. You cannot measure without first defining metrics, and you cannot test without a dataset.
source_topic: Model evaluation workflow, Step Functions, quality gates

topic: Amazon A2I — human review for low-confidence FM outputs
question_text: A medical document processing system uses an FM to extract clinical entities from patient records. The team needs to route low-confidence extractions to human reviewers before they enter the downstream database. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this human-in-the-loop review workflow?

options.text: Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) — integrates with Bedrock/SageMaker to route low-confidence predictions to a human review workflow
Amazon Rekognition — auto-approves all predictions without human review
AWS Step Functions — builds workflows but has no built-in human review UI or worker task routing
Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth — labels new training data, not production inference outputs

explanation: Amazon A2I provides a managed human review loop: it catches low-confidence model predictions and routes them to a workforce (private team, Mechanical Turk, or AWS Marketplace vendors) via a purpose-built review UI. Step Functions can orchestrate workflows but has no built-in human review task management or worker portal. Ground Truth labels training data. Rekognition does not have a human-in-the-loop review capability.
source_topic: Amazon A2I, human-in-the-loop, low-confidence review workflow

topic: Amazon Kendra vs Bedrock Knowledge Bases
question_text: A company has an existing Amazon Kendra index for enterprise search and wants to understand when to migrate to Bedrock Knowledge Bases for a RAG use case versus keeping Kendra. Which statement is MOST accurate?

options.text: Bedrock Knowledge Bases is the recommended new-build path for GenAI RAG; Kendra GenAI Index is closing to new customers in July 2026, making Bedrock Knowledge Bases the forward-looking choice
Kendra is always preferable to Bedrock Knowledge Bases for all RAG workloads
Both services are identical and the choice makes no difference
Kendra is being replaced by Amazon Lex for all search use cases

explanation: Amazon Kendra GenAI Index is closing to new customers on July 30, 2026. AWS's recommended new-build path for GenAI RAG is Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, which provides native vector search integration, multiple data source connectors, and tight coupling with Bedrock FMs. Kendra is not always preferable, the two services are not identical, and Lex is a conversational AI service unrelated to document search.
source_topic: Amazon Kendra deprecation, Bedrock Knowledge Bases, RAG service selection

topic: ROUGE BLEU BERTScore evaluation metric selection
question_text: A team is evaluating a fine-tuned model that translates English legal documents to French. They have reference translations and want an automated metric. Which evaluation metric is MOST appropriate for machine translation quality?

options.text: ROUGE — recall-oriented text overlap metric
BLEU — n-gram precision metric designed for machine translation evaluation
Perplexity — measures model prediction confidence
BERTScore — semantic similarity metric

explanation: BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) is the standard metric for machine translation — it measures n-gram precision of generated translations against human reference translations. ROUGE is designed for summarisation (recall-focused). Perplexity measures how well the model predicts the next token — a training quality metric, not output correctness. BERTScore measures semantic similarity and is better for open-ended text quality assessment.
source_topic: BLEU metric for machine translation evaluation

topic: ROUGE BLEU BERTScore evaluation metric selection
question_text: A team is evaluating a GenAI model that summarises long customer support tickets into brief summaries. They have human-written reference summaries. Which metric BEST measures how well the generated summaries capture the key information from reference summaries?

options.text: BLEU — n-gram precision for translation
Perplexity — model prediction confidence
ROUGE — recall-oriented overlap metric designed for summarisation evaluation
BOLD — bias in language generation

explanation: ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) is specifically designed for summarisation evaluation — it measures the overlap between generated summaries and reference summaries, with a focus on recall (how much of the reference content is captured). BLEU measures translation precision. Perplexity measures prediction confidence during training. BOLD measures demographic bias in generated text.
source_topic: ROUGE metric for text summarisation evaluation

topic: ROUGE BLEU BERTScore evaluation metric selection
question_text: A team evaluates a GenAI model that rewrites formal legal text into plain language. The rewrites are semantically correct but use different words than the reference texts, so ROUGE scores are low despite high human ratings. Which metric BETTER captures semantic equivalence?

options.text: BLEU — n-gram overlap precision
ROUGE-L — longest common subsequence
BERTScore — embedding-based semantic similarity that captures meaning regardless of exact wording
Perplexity — model fluency score

explanation: BERTScore uses contextual embeddings (from BERT/similar models) to measure the semantic similarity between generated and reference text — capturing meaning even when different words are used. This explains why paraphrased plain-language rewrites can score high on BERTScore despite low BLEU/ROUGE (which require word overlap). BLEU and ROUGE are both word-overlap based. Perplexity measures prediction confidence, not output quality.
source_topic: BERTScore for semantic similarity in paraphrase evaluation

topic: ROUGE BLEU BERTScore evaluation metric selection
question_text: A team trains a new language model and wants to measure how well it predicts text sequences during training — specifically to compare whether training on Dataset A or Dataset B produces a better base model. Which metric measures training quality?

options.text: ROUGE — summarisation quality
BLEU — translation quality
Perplexity — measures how well the model predicts the next token; lower perplexity indicates a better-fitting model
BERTScore — semantic similarity for output evaluation

explanation: Perplexity measures how 'surprised' the model is by test sequences — lower perplexity indicates the model has better learned the statistical patterns of the language. It is used for comparing language model training quality between different datasets, architectures, or training runs. Important exam note: Perplexity does NOT measure hallucination or output correctness. ROUGE, BLEU, and BERTScore all evaluate generated outputs against reference text.
source_topic: Perplexity for language model training quality comparison

question_text: A company wants to automatically evaluate the factual accuracy, relevance, and coherence of 10,000 Bedrock-generated customer service responses. Human review is too expensive and slow. What is the MOST scalable automated approach?

options.text: ROUGE score comparison against a reference corpus
LLM-as-a-Judge: use a separate calibrated FM (via Bedrock evaluation jobs) to score each response against a rubric for accuracy, relevance, and coherence
CloudWatch Metrics for response time — faster responses indicate higher quality
Amazon Comprehend sentiment analysis on all responses

explanation: LLM-as-a-Judge uses a secondary FM to score primary model outputs against a detailed rubric — this scales to 10,000+ evaluations automatically via Bedrock evaluation jobs, producing consistent quality scores. Bedrock Model Evaluations natively supports this approach. ROUGE requires reference text and measures overlap, not nuanced quality. Response time has no correlation with quality. Comprehend sentiment is NLP analysis, not factual accuracy evaluation.
source_topic: LLM-as-a-Judge with Bedrock evaluation jobs at scale

question_text: A team needs to systematically compare three Bedrock models (Claude Haiku, Claude Sonnet, Amazon Nova Lite) on their specific use case: customer complaint classification. They want automated scoring across accuracy, robustness, and cost. Which AWS service provides this side-by-side model comparison?

options.text: SageMaker Experiments — tracks training run comparisons
Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluations — automated comparative evaluation of multiple FMs on the same dataset
AWS Cost Explorer — compares per-token costs across models
Amazon CloudWatch dashboards — shows per-model latency comparison

explanation: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluations is purpose-built for systematic, automated side-by-side comparison of multiple FMs against your own datasets. You define evaluation criteria (accuracy, robustness, cost), select the models, provide the dataset, and get a structured comparison report. SageMaker Experiments tracks ML training runs. Cost Explorer shows billing data only. CloudWatch shows operational metrics — none provide the ML quality evaluation framework that Model Evaluations does.
source_topic: Bedrock Model Evaluations for side-by-side FM comparison

question_text: A RAG system is producing inaccurate answers. The team needs to determine whether the problem is (A) the retrieval step returning wrong documents, or (B) the FM generating a poor answer despite good retrieved context. What is the CORRECT evaluation approach to isolate the failure?

options.text: Run end-to-end evaluation with RetrieveAndGenerate and score final answers only
Run retrieval-only evaluation first using the Retrieve API to assess whether correct chunks are returned; if retrieval is good, then evaluate generation quality separately
Check CloudWatch latency metrics to determine which component is slower
Fine-tune the FM to improve overall answer quality

explanation: The key principle: 'Unsure whether errors come from retrieval or generation → Run retrieve-only evaluation first.' The Bedrock Retrieve API returns only retrieved chunks without generation — enabling evaluation of whether the right documents are being found. If retrieval is good but answers are wrong, the problem is in generation (fix: improve prompts, switch models). If retrieval is wrong, fix the chunking/embedding/search. End-to-end evaluation (A) can't isolate which component failed. Latency doesn't diagnose quality. Fine-tuning is premature before identifying the root cause.
source_topic: RAG two-part evaluation: retrieve-only then retrieve-and-generate

question_text: A team wants to evaluate their Bedrock Agent across multiple test scenarios including happy paths, edge cases, and adversarial inputs. They want to compare two agent configurations (different system prompts) and score tool selection accuracy and task completion rate. Which service is purpose-built for this?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluations — for FM model comparisons
Amazon Bedrock Agent Evaluations — specifically designed for evaluating agent tool selection, reasoning, and task completion
SageMaker Clarify — for bias detection in ML models
AWS Step Functions execution history — logs agent steps

explanation: Amazon Bedrock Agent Evaluations is purpose-built for evaluating Bedrock Agents: it tests the agent's conversation flows against predefined success criteria, evaluates tool selection accuracy, reasoning quality, and task completion rates across multiple scenarios (happy path and edge cases). It also supports comparing two agent configurations. Model Evaluations compares FMs, not agents. Clarify detects training data bias. Step Functions history logs workflow execution but doesn't provide quality scoring.
source_topic: Bedrock Agent Evaluations for agent-specific quality testing

question_text: A team evaluates their RAG retrieval system using Precision@5 (P@5). For 100 test queries, they find P@5 = 0.4. What does this mean and what is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: 40% of all documents in the index are relevant — the index is too large
On average, 2 out of the top 5 retrieved chunks are relevant — poor retrieval precision, likely caused by suboptimal embeddings, chunking, or index parameters
40% of queries return at least one relevant result — recall is poor
The FM uses 40% of retrieved context to generate answers — the rest is ignored

explanation: Precision@k means: for the top k retrieved results, what fraction are relevant? P@5 = 0.4 means on average 2 out of 5 retrieved chunks are relevant — 60% are irrelevant noise sent to the FM. This is likely caused by: poor chunking (chunks that are too large/small), suboptimal embedding model, overly broad search, or missing metadata filters. P@5 doesn't measure total index relevance, all-query coverage, or FM context utilisation.
source_topic: Precision@k for measuring RAG retrieval quality

topic: SageMaker Ground Truth — training data labeling
question_text: A company wants to build a 'golden dataset' for ongoing GenAI evaluation by having domain experts (medical professionals) annotate 5,000 clinical question-answer pairs as correct/incorrect/partially-correct. They need a managed workflow for task assignment, annotation collection, and quality control. Which AWS service provides this?

options.text: Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) — for reviewing live ML predictions
Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth — managed data labelling with private workforce, quality control, and active learning
Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluations — for automated FM comparison
AWS Mechanical Turk — crowdsourced annotations without managed workflows

explanation: SageMaker Ground Truth provides the full managed labelling workflow: task assignment to private workforce (medical professionals), annotation collection, consensus-based quality control (multiple raters, gold standard examples), and active learning to reduce labelling cost for easy cases. A2I reviews live ML predictions, not batch dataset creation. Bedrock Model Evaluations uses automated scoring, not human annotation. Mechanical Turk is a crowdsourcing marketplace (accessible through Ground Truth) but without the managed quality control Ground Truth provides.
source_topic: SageMaker Ground Truth for managed expert dataset annotation

question_text: A team wants to deploy an updated Bedrock prompt version to production but is cautious about potential regressions. They want to first expose only 5% of production traffic to the new prompt while monitoring error rates and user satisfaction, before gradually increasing to 100%. This describes which deployment strategy?

options.text: Blue/green deployment — switch all traffic at once between two environments
Canary testing — deploy to a small subset of users first, monitor metrics, then gradually roll out
A/B testing — split traffic 50/50 between two variants for statistical comparison
Shadow testing — send all traffic to both but show users only the original

explanation: Canary testing deploys a new version to a small subset of users (5%) while monitoring closely for errors or regressions, then gradually increases the percentage. This limits blast radius if the new prompt causes issues. Blue/green switches all traffic simultaneously. A/B testing splits traffic 50/50 for statistical comparison (not a gradual rollout). Shadow testing runs the new version hidden from users for silent comparison.
source_topic: Canary testing for safe gradual GenAI prompt rollout

question_text: After deploying a new version of a Bedrock-powered application, the team wants to immediately validate that the new deployment doesn't exhibit semantic drift — that responses to standard questions haven't meaningfully changed in meaning from the previous version. What validation approach detects semantic drift?

options.text: Compare response character lengths between old and new versions
Use BERTScore or cosine embedding similarity to compare new responses against baseline responses for a golden question set — alert if semantic distance exceeds threshold
Check CloudWatch error rate metrics for the new deployment
Use Amazon Inspector to scan new Lambda functions for code vulnerabilities

explanation: Semantic drift detection computes the embedding similarity between current responses and baseline (known-good) responses for a standard question set. If the semantic distance exceeds a threshold, it signals that response meaning has shifted — even if responses are grammatically correct. BERTScore or cosine similarity are the correct tools. Character length comparison (A) misses semantic changes. CloudWatch error rates detect technical failures, not quality drift. Inspector scans for security vulnerabilities.
source_topic: BERTScore/cosine similarity for semantic drift detection post-deployment

question_text: A model evaluation pipeline for a regulated industry application requires: automated scoring, human approval gating before model promotion, and an immutable decision record. Which combination of AWS services implements this complete pipeline?

options.text: CloudWatch Dashboard + SNS email notification + manual DynamoDB update
Bedrock Model Evaluations (automated scoring) → Step Functions (gate on quality threshold; waitForTaskToken for human approval) → SageMaker Model Registry (record approved model version)
Bedrock Guardrails (content filtering) + Lambda (deployment) + S3 (reports)
Amazon A2I (human review) + Glue ETL (process results) + RDS (store approval)

explanation: The complete regulated evaluation pipeline: (1) Bedrock Model Evaluations runs automated scoring against quality metrics. (2) Step Functions gates on the score threshold — if passing, uses waitForTaskToken to pause for human approval via API Gateway. (3) On approval, the model version is promoted in SageMaker Model Registry (immutable, versioned record). CloudWatch/SNS + manual DynamoDB lacks the automated quality gate and structured workflow. Guardrails is a safety tool, not an evaluation pipeline. A2I + Glue + RDS lacks the structured evaluation and model registry.
source_topic: Full evaluation pipeline: Model Evaluations + Step Functions + Model Registry

question_text: A team is setting up a continuous evaluation workflow that runs nightly. Place the following steps in the correct order: (1) Store eval dataset in S3, (2) Run Bedrock Model Evaluation job with LLM-as-judge, (3) Apply quality gate via Step Functions Choice state, (4) If passing, promote model in Model Registry, (5) Send SNS alert on pass/fail. Which sequence is correct?
explanation: The logical sequence is: (1) Store evaluation dataset in S3 (prerequisite). (2) Run Bedrock Model Evaluation job using that dataset. (3) Step Functions Choice state evaluates whether scores meet the quality threshold. (4) If threshold met, promote the model in Model Registry. (5) Send SNS notification of pass/fail result. The alert happens after the decision (not before or during). This is the AWS-recommended continuous evaluation workflow.
source_topic: Continuous evaluation workflow step ordering

question_text: A team discovers that after updating their system prompt, the FM started including disclaimers in responses where it previously didn't. They want a systematic way to detect such output format/content changes after each future deployment. What approach enables this?

options.text: Monitor CloudWatch ModelLatency for changes after each deployment
After each deployment, automatically run a golden question set and diff current outputs against previous baseline outputs using string comparison or LLM-as-judge
Use Amazon Macie to scan new responses for format changes
Use AWS Config to detect changes in the system prompt configuration

explanation: Output diffing is the practice of comparing current model outputs against baseline outputs for the same standard inputs after each deployment. String diff catches format changes (like added disclaimers); LLM-as-judge captures semantic changes. This is implemented in a Step Functions post-deployment validation workflow. Latency monitoring detects performance regressions, not content changes. Macie discovers sensitive data. Config tracks resource configurations.
source_topic: Output diffing for post-deployment response change detection

question_text: A GenAI product manager asks: 'We collect thumbs up/down feedback. Is this enough as the primary quality evaluation signal for our production model?' What is the CORRECT assessment?

options.text: Yes — user feedback is the ground truth for model quality

No — user feedback alone is insufficient; it is noisy, subject to bias, and doesn't scale for systematic comparison. It should supplement automated evaluation (Bedrock Model Evaluations + LLM-as-judge) not replace it
Yes — if the thumbs up rate exceeds 80%, the model is production-ready
No — user feedback should be completely ignored as it is too subjective

explanation: User feedback is valuable as a continuous improvement signal but has significant limitations: it is noisy (users give inconsistent ratings), biased (users rate positively for fluent responses even if factually wrong), and not ground truth for model comparison. Automated evaluation (Bedrock Model Evaluations, LLM-as-judge, golden datasets) provides more reliable, scalable, and reproducible quality assessment. The recommended approach combines both: automated evaluation for systematic comparison + user feedback for ongoing production signals.
source_topic: User feedback limitations — not a substitute for automated evaluation
